issues.legal_issue: Judicial review of a domestic arbitral award is confined to the statutory grounds for setting it aside and does not permit an appeal on the merits.
material_facts: The dispute arose from a domestic arbitration under a concession agreement.
The award was challenged under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, and the challenge was considered on appeal under Section 37.
The High Court reassessed factual matters and contractual interpretation when setting aside parts of the award.
issues.conclusion: Courts reviewing an arbitral award must remain within the limited grounds for intervention and must not reappreciate evidence or substitute their view for a reasonable possible view taken by the tribunal.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 5, 34(2), 34(2-A), and 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 limit judicial intervention. Patent illegality must go to the root of the matter and does not include mere legal error or reappreciation of evidence; a view that is not even possible, a contract interpretation no fair-minded or reasonable person would adopt, jurisdictional error, absence of reasons, or a finding based on no evidence or ignoring vital evidence may justify intervention. The Court relied on Ssangyong Engineering and Construction Company Limited v. National Highways Authority of India, Associate Builders v. Delhi Development Authority, Uttarakhand Purv Sainik Kalyan Nigam Limited v. Northern Coal Field Limited, Bhaven Construction v. Executive Engineer Sardar Sarovar Narmada Nigam Ltd., Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Limited v. Dewan Chand Ram Saran, and Renusagar Power Co. Ltd. v. General Electric Co.

rule.if: domestic_arbitral_award_challenge and court_reviewing_award and (award_has_statutory_ground_for_interference or not award_has_statutory_ground_for_interference)

predicates.domestic_arbitral_award_challenge: A party challenges a domestic arbitral award in court.
predicates.court_reviewing_award: A court examines the challenged award rather than deciding the underlying dispute anew.
predicates.award_has_statutory_ground_for_interfere: The award has a defect of the kind that permits a court to set it aside.
predicates.not_award_has_statutory_ground_for_inter: The award does not have a defect of the kind that permits a court to set it aside.

issues.definition: When a court reviews a domestic arbitral award, its decision is limited to whether a recognized ground for interference exists, rather than a fresh decision on the merits.

issues.legal_issue: An arbitral tribunal's supported finding that contractual defects were not cured within the applicable cure period cannot be displaced merely because a later safety clearance permitted operations to resume.
material_facts: The concessionaire gave notice identifying defects in the civil structure and requiring them to be cured within the contractual cure period.
The tribunal found that substantial defects remained uncured and that effective steps had not been taken within that period, relying on evidence about cracks, twists, and other deficiencies.
A later safety certificate permitted operations to resume subject to speed restrictions and monitoring conditions.
The tribunal treated the safety question and the contractual question of timely cure as distinct and found the termination notice valid.
The High Court set aside that finding, relying in part on the later certificate and subsequent operation of the line.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to set aside the tribunal's finding on the validity of termination; the tribunal's factual conclusions and possible interpretation of the cure provision were not shown to be perverse or patently illegal.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 34 and 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, courts cannot reappreciate evidence or replace a possible interpretation of a contract adopted by the tribunal. A later safety clearance does not by itself establish that contractual defects were cured within the earlier cure period. The Court relied on Ssangyong Engineering and Construction Company Limited v. National Highways Authority of India, Associate Builders v. Delhi Development Authority, and State of Rajasthan v. Puri Construction Co. Ltd.

rule.if: appeal_from_order_setting_aside_arbitral_award and tribunal_found_contractual_defects_uncured_within_cure_period and tribunal_relied_on_evidence and later_safety_clearance_was_conditional and tribunal_adopted_possible_contract_interpretation

predicates.appeal_from_order_setting_aside_arbitral: A party appeals from a court order that set aside an arbitral award.
predicates.tribunal_found_contractual_defects_uncur: The tribunal found that contractual defects were not cured, or effective steps to cure them were not taken, within the applicable cure period.
predicates.tribunal_relied_on_evidence: The tribunal based its finding on evidence presented in the arbitration.
predicates.later_safety_clearance_was_conditional: A competent safety authority later permitted operations subject to restrictions or continued monitoring.
predicates.tribunal_adopted_possible_contract_inter: The tribunal adopted a reasonable possible interpretation of the parties' contract.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns an order setting aside an award, and the tribunal made an evidence-based finding of untimely cure using a possible contractual interpretation, a later conditional safety clearance does not justify setting aside that finding.

issues.legal_issue: A tribunal's reasonable interpretation of a contractual definition of equity may not be replaced by a court's competing interpretation when calculating contractual termination payment.
material_facts: The concession agreement defined equity to include funds advanced by a consortium member or shareholder to meet the concessionaire's capital costs.
The tribunal treated the promoter's advance as equity for the contractual calculation of adjusted equity, despite its later classification as subordinated debt in company records.
The tribunal considered the relevant agreement and evidence, including the board resolution concerning the change in classification.
The High Court substituted its interpretation and set aside the resulting termination payment calculation.
issues.conclusion: The tribunal's interpretation was a reasonable possible view, and the High Court was not entitled to substitute its own view; the tribunal's computation of termination payment was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Contract interpretation is primarily for the arbitral tribunal. Under Section 28(3) and Section 34(2-A) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, a court may not set aside an award merely because another contractual interpretation is possible; intervention requires, among other things, an interpretation no fair-minded or reasonable person would adopt or another recognized ground for setting aside. The Court relied on Ssangyong Engineering and Construction Company Limited v. National Highways Authority of India and Associate Builders v. Delhi Development Authority.

predicates.appeal_from_order_setting_aside_arbitral: A party appeals from a court order that set aside an arbitral award.
predicates.contract_defines_equity_to_include_proje: The contract treats qualifying funding advances as equity for the relevant contractual calculation.
predicates.tribunal_considered_relevant_contract_an: The tribunal considered the contractual terms and material evidence relevant to the calculation.
predicates.tribunal_interpretation_is_reasonably_po: The tribunal's interpretation is one a reasonable decision-maker could adopt.

issues.definition: If the contract includes project-funding advances in equity and the tribunal considered the relevant terms and evidence, a reasonably possible interpretation must not be replaced merely because a court prefers another view.

issues.legal_issue: Participation in post-notice reconciliation and continued operation of a project without prejudice does not waive a party's right to terminate for an uncured contractual default.
material_facts: After issuing the termination notice, the concessionaire participated in meetings and reconciliation efforts concerning the defects.
The tribunal found that this participation and the subsequent operation of the line were without prejudice.
The tribunal rejected the contention that the concessionaire had waived termination or was estopped from relying on the default.
The High Court declined to interfere with that finding, and the Supreme Court agreed.
issues.conclusion: The tribunal's finding that the termination right was not waived was correctly left undisturbed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the limited review of arbitral awards under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 and held that the tribunal's supported finding on waiver was not a basis for court interference.

predicates.challenge_to_arbitral_award: A party asks a court to interfere with an arbitral award.
predicates.party_participated_in_reconciliation_aft: A party took part in meetings or reconciliation efforts after giving a termination notice.
predicates.party_continued_operations_without_preju: A party continued operating the project while expressly preserving its position.
predicates.tribunal_found_no_waiver: The tribunal found that the party had not relinquished its termination right.

issues.definition: When a party participates in reconciliation and continues operations without prejudice, and the tribunal finds no relinquishment, those actions do not waive the termination right.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not adjudicate a specific-performance issue that was not challenged before the High Court.
material_facts: The tribunal refused a direction requiring the concessionaire to perform its operating obligations.
The High Court recorded that the tribunal's refusal had not been challenged before it.
The Supreme Court therefore declined to decide the specific-performance issue.
issues.conclusion: The Court did not adjudicate the issue of specific performance.
issues.legal_principle: The Court confined its consideration to issues properly raised and challenged before the High Court; it gave no separate substantive ruling on specific performance.

predicates.appeal_before_supreme_court: A party brings an appeal before the Supreme Court concerning a dispute decided in lower courts.
predicates.issue_not_challenged_before_high_court: The party did not challenge the relevant ruling before the High Court.

issues.definition: If an issue was not challenged before the High Court, the Supreme Court does not adjudicate it in the later appeal.

issues.legal_issue: A contractual interest award should not be disturbed when the High Court has considered the relevant contractual terms and no basis for further interference is shown.
material_facts: The tribunal awarded interest on the termination payment in accordance with the concession agreement.
The opposing party argued that the interest award would result in unjust enrichment.
The High Court considered the relevant contractual provisions and refused to interfere with the tribunal's interest ruling.
The Supreme Court found no cause to disturb that decision.
issues.conclusion: The interest award was left undisturbed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the contractual terms governing interest and the limited scope for judicial interference with an arbitral award under Sections 34 and 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.

rule.if: appeal_concerning_arbitral_interest_award and contract_provides_basis_for_interest and high_court_considered_relevant_contractual_terms and no_further_ground_for_interference_shown

predicates.appeal_concerning_arbitral_interest_awar: An appeal asks the court to interfere with interest awarded by an arbitral tribunal.
predicates.contract_provides_basis_for_interest: The parties' contract contains terms governing the interest at issue.
predicates.high_court_considered_relevant_contractu: The High Court considered the contractual terms relevant to the interest award.
predicates.no_further_ground_for_interference_shown: The appealing party has not established a basis for the Supreme Court to disturb the ruling.

issues.definition: An interest award based on contractual terms is upheld when the High Court has considered those terms and no further ground for interference is shown.
